blocks.text: 7.4.1. Limitations of Traditional String Literals

At 02:00 the nightly cleanup job logged out every user of the shop. It was meant to delete only expired sessions, and its `DELETE` had been copied from the DBA's script, comment included, one `"..." +` per line. Nothing failed: the statement ran and reported a row count.

A traditional string literal holds one line of text, and quotes, backslashes and line breaks inside it are written as escapes. Multi-line SQL, JSON and HTML pay for that, in four ways, one per heading below.
Every Quote and Backslash Is Written Twice, and a Wrong Backslash Can Still Compile
Inside a literal, `"` is written `\"` and `\` is written `\\`. JSON that itself contains an escaped quote gets both layers:

String json = "{\"sku\": \"A-17\", \"note\": \"say \\\"hi\\\"\"}";
System.out.println(json);
That is hard to review, but a dropped `\"` usually fails to compile. A dropped backslash fails only when the letter after it is not a known escape:
Pause before the next run: a Windows path and a regex for the whole word `cat`, each written with single backslashes. Do they compile?

path: length 16, char 2 is 9, char 6 is 10
written "\\bcat\\b": 1 match
written "\bcat\b":   0 matches, first char 8

Both compile. `\t` and `\n` are valid escapes, so the path holds a tab (9) and a newline (10), and any code that opens it looks for a folder that doesn't exist. `\b` is a valid escape too: backspace, U+0008. The regex engine never sees a word boundary, so the pattern matches nothing, and an alert built on it never fires.

`javac` processes the escapes first, and only what is left reaches the regex engine, the JSON parser or the file system. Each backslash the inner language needs is `\\` in the source, and a single one is either an error or a different character, depending on the letter after it. The Reference lists the letters that compile.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Value Split Across Lines Has a Seam at Every `+`, and a Missing `\n` or Space There Changes It

A literal can't contain a line break (`javac` says `unclosed string literal`), so a statement copied from a script becomes one literal per line, joined with `+`. These two came from the cleanup job and from a report:

String cleanup =
        "DELETE FROM sessions " +
        "-- keep sessions that are still valid " +
        "WHERE expires_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 00:00:00'";
String report =
        "SELECT id, total" +
        "FROM orders WHERE status = 'OPEN'";
Printed, then run against an in-memory H2 database holding three sessions, two of them expired:

DELETE FROM sessions -- keep sessions that are still valid WHERE expires_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 00:00:00'
SELECT id, totalFROM orders WHERE status = 'OPEN'
cleanup deleted 3 of 3 sessions, 2 had expired
report: Column "ID" not found; SQL statement:
SELECT id, totalFROM orders WHERE status = 'OPEN' [42122-224]

The value holds exactly what is between the quotes. The line breaks you see in the editor are outside them, so they are not in the string. In the script, the comment ended at the end of its line; in the string there is no end of line, and `--` comments out the `WHERE`. A `DELETE` without a condition is valid SQL, so the database deleted every row and reported success. The second seam lost a space, and fails only when it runs, with an error that names a column.

The `+` itself costs nothing at run time: both expressions are constant, and `javac` folds each into one string (`javap` shows a single `ldc` per statement; unit 1.4.2). The cost is that every seam needs its `\n` or its space by hand, and a reviewer reading the Java sees the layout of the source, not of the value. If you build multi-line text from literals, end every piece with `\n`, so comments stay terminated and the value prints the way the source looks.
`\n` Is Always a Line Feed; `%n`, `println` and `lineSeparator()` Follow the Platform

Which newline goes at the end of each piece? The same program, run as it is and with `line.separator` set to `\r\n`, the value Windows uses (`hex` prints the UTF-8 bytes; `buf` holds what a `PrintStream`'s `println("ok")` wrote):

$ java LineEnds
"ok\n"                   6f 6b 0a
String.format("ok%n")    6f 6b 0a
"ok" + lineSeparator()   6f 6b 0a
println("ok")            6f 6b 0a
expected.equals(actual): true
$ java -Dline.separator=$'\r\n' LineEnds
"ok\n"                   6f 6b 0a
String.format("ok%n")    6f 6b 0d 0a
"ok" + lineSeparator()   6f 6b 0d 0a
println("ok")            6f 6b 0d 0a
expected.equals(actual): false

`
` is decided by `javac`: it is U+000A in the class file, whatever machine runs it. `%n`, `println` and `System.lineSeparator()` use the `line.separator` property as the JVM started with it, which the javadoc gives as `"
"` on Unix and `"
"` on Windows.

A test that compares a report built with `%n` against an expected `"...
"` passes on the Linux CI and fails on a colleague's Windows laptop. In the other direction, a format that requires CR LF, such as HTTP/1.1 headers, SMTP or CSV per RFC 4180, gets bare LF from `%n` on a Linux server. Choose by where the text goes: a format with fixed line endings gets the escape it requires (`
` or `
`), and only text for the local console or a local file gets `%n`.
<!-- practice 2 -->
A Text Block Removes the Escaped Quotes and the Seams, Not the Backslashes or the Values

A text block (Java 15, unit 7.1.3) is one literal between `"""` delimiters that may span lines. Here is the JSON, once concatenated and twice as a block, one of them with a placeholder in the style of other languages:

The quotes need no escape and the line breaks are real ones, so there are no seams to get wrong: the cleanup `DELETE` written as a block, one source line per SQL line, deleted 2 of the 3 sessions. `filled` is an ordinary `String`, equal to the concatenated one.

A text block has no interpolation: `${sku}` is six characters of text, and values still go in through `formatted`, `+`, or, for SQL, bind parameters (unit 7.4.5). String templates (JEPs 430 and 459) were previews in Java 21 and 22 and were then withdrawn: `javac` 21 rejects `STR."..."` without `--enable-preview`, and `javac` 25 rejects its `\{` as an illegal escape. And a block still processes escapes, so the regex problem of the first section is unchanged:

A block's line breaks are `\n` on every platform, so the previous section still applies when one is compared with output written with `%n`. How the delimiters and the trailing newline work is unit 7.4.2, indentation is 7.4.3, and the block-only escapes are 7.4.4.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **Every quote and backslash is written twice.** Unknown escapes fail to compile, but `\t`, `\n`, `\b`, `\r`, `\f`, `\s` and octal ones such as `\1` compile and silently change a path or a regex.

**Text split across lines has a seam at every `+`.** A missing `\n` lets a SQL `--` comment swallow the rest of the statement, which then reports success; a missing space joins two words, and the statement fails only when it runs. The `+` of literals is folded at compile time and costs nothing.
**`\n` is fixed; `%n`, `println` and `lineSeparator()` follow the platform.** Write the escape a format requires, and keep `%n` for local output.
**A text block removes escaped quotes and seams.** It still processes backslash escapes and has no interpolation; string templates were withdrawn.

**Escapes a traditional literal accepts (Java 21):**

rows: the octal character code: `\0` is U+0000, `\1` is U+0001 (not a regex backreference), `\101` is `A`
a Unicode escape, translated before the source is read as tokens (unit 7.4.4)

blocks.text: **Line endings:**

rows: `\n` in a literal or a text block
the `line.separator` property at JVM start: `0a` on Unix, `0d 0a` on Windows

blocks.text: Challenges

items: Search a codebase you know for `" +` followed on the next line by SQL. Which seams have neither `\n` nor a space, and which statements contain `--`?
A service writes CSV that a partner parses with a strict RFC 4180 reader, and the tests run on Linux only. How would you make the tests notice a `%n` slipping into the writer?
Your team keeps large queries in `.sql` resource files instead of literals. Which of this page's costs does that remove, and what does it add?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why a Text Block Still Processes Escapes

A text block could have been raw, with every backslash kept as written. Java chose to process the same escapes as a traditional literal, so moving a literal into a block never changes what an escape means, and a block can still say `\t` or `\r\n` where an invisible character is needed. The cost is the one the first section measured: a regex or a Windows path in a block doubles its backslashes exactly as before, and a single `\b` is still a backspace.
